lessons.title: The Big Bang Theory: Launching the Phenomenon

quiz.prompt: A learner stands on the escarpment above Nakuru on a moonless night, switches off the torch and looks up. Which statement best describes how the sky looks to the unaided eye?
choices: The sky looks calm and unchanging, as if it has always been this way
The Milky Way band changes shape every minute
Stars can be seen exploding every few seconds
The stars are visibly moving apart from each other as the learner watches
quiz.rationale: The anchoring phenomenon is that the night sky looks still, permanent and ancient to direct observation, even though scientists claim the universe had a beginning. Nothing visibly expands or explodes while we watch.
quiz.placement: Rift Valley night-sky image and narrative read aloud (Predict phase)

quiz.prompt: According to the Big Bang Theory, approximately how long ago did the universe begin?
choices: About 13.8 million years ago
About 13.8 billion years ago
About 6 000 years ago
About 4.6 billion years ago
quiz.rationale: The Big Bang Theory proposes that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, extremely dense singularity.
quiz.placement: Kurzgesagt video 'The Big Bang: How Did Everything Begin?' and Khan Academy article 'The Big Bang'

quiz.prompt: A class looks at the night sky above Nairobi and discusses what they know. Which statement is a scientific inference rather than a direct observation?
choices: The Moon looks large and bright
The Milky Way appears as a band of light across the sky
The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago
Jupiter appears low in the east tonight
quiz.rationale: We can see Jupiter, the Moon and the Milky Way directly. Nobody can watch the universe begin, so its age is concluded from evidence and reasoning.
quiz.placement: Evidence Collection Table and discussion of 'Evidence We Found'

quiz.prompt: A learner asks: 'If the Big Bang happened 13.8 billion years ago, why does the night sky above Nairobi look so calm and permanent tonight?' What is the best response at this point in the unit?
choices: The Big Bang happened far away from Earth, so we cannot see any effects
The universe stopped expanding and became permanent after the Big Bang
This is an open question that has not been explained yet, and the class will investigate it through the unit
The stars all stopped moving soon after the Big Bang
quiz.rationale: In this lesson the question is deliberately left unanswered and is carried forward as the driving question of the unit. The other choices are guesses that the lesson has not supported.
quiz.placement: Teacher zooms out after the CER discussion: 'why does this sky look so still?'

quiz.prompt: In a Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) explanation about how the universe began, which description fits 'evidence'?
choices: Specific information from a source, such as the video or article, that supports the claim
Your opinion about which answer is best
How much you like the theory
A restatement of the question in your own words
quiz.rationale: Evidence is specific information, such as a fact or data from a source, that supports the claim. Opinions and vague restatements are not evidence.
quiz.placement: CER written explanation: 'Make a claim about how the universe began'

quiz.prompt: Which of these questions for the Driving Question Board is the most specific and scientifically testable?
choices: Why is everything so big?
What is space?
Is the sky beautiful?
How do scientists measure the age of the universe?
quiz.rationale: A good DQB question is specific and can be investigated with evidence. 'How do scientists measure the age of the universe?' is focused. The others are vague or about opinion.
quiz.placement: Learners write questions on sticky notes and post them on the Driving Question Board

quiz.prompt: A learner draws a timeline from the Big Bang to tonight's sky above Nairobi. Which event should be at the far left, as the earliest event?
choices: The Solar System forms
Learners look at the night sky
The Milky Way is seen from Earth tonight
The Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago
quiz.rationale: The timeline starts at the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago, and ends with tonight's sky. Every other event comes after it.
quiz.placement: MY UNIVERSE MODEL, Version 1: timeline diagram from the Big Bang to tonight's sky

lessons.title: Evolution of the Universe: From the Big Bang to the Structured Night Sky

quiz.prompt: Scientists say the universe began in an event called the Big Bang. About how long ago did this happen?
choices: About 380,000 years ago
About 200 million years ago
About 4.6 billion years ago
About 13.8 billion years ago
quiz.rationale: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. 4.6 billion years is when the Solar System formed, 380,000 years is when the first atoms formed, and 200 million years is when the first stars ignited.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share and Prediction Wall (if the universe began 13.8 billion years ago from a single point)

quiz.prompt: Which list shows these events in the correct order, from earliest to latest?
choices: Quark-gluon plasma, then protons and neutrons form, then first atoms form, then first stars ignite
First atoms form, then protons and neutrons form, then quark-gluon plasma, then first stars
Protons and neutrons form, then the Solar System forms, then first stars ignite, then first atoms form
Quark-gluon plasma, then first stars ignite, then first atoms form, then protons and neutrons form
quiz.rationale: The universe began as a hot quark-gluon plasma. Protons and neutrons formed next, then atoms about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, then the first stars at about 200 million years. Atoms cannot form before protons, and stars cannot form before atoms.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Big Bang Timeline Construction (Cosmic Events Card Set)

quiz.prompt: A 2-metre rope is used as a straight, linear timeline of 13.8 billion years, with the Big Bang at one end and tonight at the other end. The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago. How far from the Big Bang end of the rope should the Solar System card be placed?
choices: About 46 cm
About 133 cm
About 92 cm
About 67 cm
quiz.rationale: The Solar System formed 13.8 - 4.6 = 9.2 billion years after the Big Bang. So the distance is 9.2 / 13.8 x 200 cm, which is about 133 cm. The 67 cm answer measures 4.6 billion years from the Big Bang end instead of from tonight.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Big Bang Timeline Construction (marking where each event falls on the 2-metre rope)

quiz.prompt: On a 2-metre rope representing 13.8 billion years, the first stars ignited about 200 million years after the Big Bang. How far from the Big Bang end of the rope do the first stars belong?
choices: 29 cm
100 cm
2.9 cm
quiz.rationale: 200 million is 0.2 billion. The fraction of the timeline is 0.2 / 13.8, and 0.2 / 13.8 x 200 cm is about 2.9 cm. This shows the first stars appeared very early on the timeline, but not within minutes of the Big Bang.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Big Bang Timeline Construction (misconception check on placing first stars)

quiz.prompt: Which type of galaxy is our home galaxy, the Milky Way?
choices: An elliptical galaxy
An irregular galaxy
A barred spiral galaxy
A single very large star cluster with no arms
quiz.rationale: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy: it has spiral arms and a bar-shaped centre. Our Solar System lies inside it.
quiz.placement: Activity B: NASA Galaxy Classification (identify the Milky Way)

quiz.prompt: The Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) is a faint glow of microwaves that reaches Earth almost equally from every direction. Why is it important evidence for the Big Bang?
choices: It is light from the first stars, which ignited a few minutes after the Big Bang
It is old light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, which suggests the early universe was hot and dense
It is sunlight reflected from the Moon and spread across the sky
It is radio signals sent by human-made satellites orbiting Earth
quiz.rationale: The CMB is the oldest light we can see. It was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang and has since been stretched into microwaves. This supports a hot, dense beginning. The first stars came much later.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher input gap (1) CMB, after the video 'Evolution of the Universe in 5 Minutes'

quiz.prompt: Dots are drawn on a balloon and the balloon is inflated. Every dot moves away from every other dot. What does this model show about the Big Bang?
choices: The Big Bang happened only to the galaxies nearest to Earth
The Big Bang was an expansion of space itself, and no galaxy is the centre of the expansion
The Big Bang stopped expanding once the first galaxies formed
The Big Bang was an explosion at one point in space, and galaxies were thrown outward from that centre
quiz.rationale: On the balloon every dot moves away from every other dot and no dot is the centre. In the same way, space itself expanded, and the universe is still expanding today. It was not an explosion inside space.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher input gap (2) Expansion, balloon demonstration

quiz.prompt: Carbon and oxygen are found in living things and on Earth. According to the evolution of the universe, where were these heavier elements made?
choices: They were made by the Moon and carried to Earth
They were all made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang
They were made inside stars and scattered into space when massive stars ended as supernovae
They were made inside the Earth after the planet formed
quiz.rationale: The Big Bang mainly produced hydrogen and helium. Stars fuse elements, and massive stars scatter carbon, oxygen, iron and others in supernovae. The Sun and Earth later formed from a gas and dust cloud enriched by earlier stars.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher input gap (3) Stars, and the Kericho farmer explanation paragraph

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'The night sky above Nairobi looks the same every night, so the universe has always been like this.' Which reply best uses the evidence from the lesson?
choices: The sky only looks unchanged because a human lifetime is a tiny sliver of the 13.8 billion years over which the universe has evolved
The sky looks unchanged because the universe is only a few thousand years old
The sky looks unchanged because the Big Bang created all the stars, planets and galaxies at the same time
The sky looks unchanged because the universe stopped expanding after the first galaxies formed
quiz.rationale: On the 2-metre rope timeline, human history is almost an invisible sliver of cosmic time. The sky seems still because we observe it for so short a time, even though the universe evolved over 13.8 billion years and is still expanding.
quiz.placement: Model Building: first model update and closing link to the anchoring phenomenon (night sky above Nairobi)

lessons.title: Classification of Celestial Bodies: Reading the Kenyan Night Sky

quiz.prompt: A student sorts the objects in a Rift Valley night-sky photograph into two groups: objects that MAKE their own light and objects that only REFLECT light. Which object belongs in the group that makes its own light?
choices: Jupiter, a planet
Venus, a planet
The Moon
Sirius, a star
quiz.rationale: Stars such as Sirius produce their own light. Planets and moons only reflect light from a star, so Venus, Jupiter and the Moon belong in the reflecting group.
quiz.placement: Predict: Rift Valley night-sky photograph, writing a type-list and deciding when two objects belong to the same category

quiz.prompt: In Stellarium, a learner sees that Venus is one of the brightest objects in the Nairobi evening sky and writes 'star' as its type. Which statement correctly explains why Venus is NOT a star?
choices: Venus is a star, but it is much closer than the other stars
Venus is too small to be seen without a telescope
Venus does not make its own light; it reflects light from the Sun, so it is a planet
Venus is brighter than every star, so it must be something different
quiz.rationale: Brightness to the eye does not decide the type of object. Venus is a planet because it only reflects sunlight, while stars make their own light.
quiz.placement: Observe: Stellarium Observation Sheet, logging Venus and classifying it using the data panel

quiz.prompt: A learner fills in the 'How I can tell' column of a Stellarium Observation Sheet for the Andromeda Galaxy. Which entry is the strongest scientific evidence for its type?
choices: 'The data panel gives its type as galaxy and its distance as millions of light-years.'
'It is in the sky near the Milky Way.'
'My friend said it is a galaxy.'
'It looks bright and fuzzy to me.'
quiz.rationale: Evidence should come from data such as type, distance and magnitude in the data panel. How bright an object looks to the eye does not show what type of object it is.
quiz.placement: Observe: Stellarium Observation Sheet, 'How I can tell (evidence from Stellarium data panel)' column

quiz.prompt: Which list puts these events in the correct order of cosmic evolution, from earliest to latest?
choices: First stars form, then the Big Bang, then galaxies, then rocky bodies
Big Bang, then first stars, then galaxies, then solar systems, then rocky bodies
Big Bang, then solar systems, then first stars, then galaxies
Solar systems form, then first stars form, then galaxies form, then the Big Bang
quiz.rationale: The sequence in the lesson is Big Bang, then first stars, then galaxies, then solar systems, then rocky bodies. Planets and rocky bodies could only form after earlier stars existed.
quiz.placement: Observe: 'Evolution of the Universe in 5 Minutes' clip paused at first stars, galaxies and solar system formation

quiz.prompt: The Milky Way band that students see on a clear night in the Rift Valley is part of which class of celestial body, and what is that class?
choices: A planet: a body that orbits a star and reflects its light
A galaxy: a huge collection of billions of stars held together in space
An asteroid: a small rocky body that orbits the Sun
A comet: an icy body with a glowing tail
quiz.rationale: The Milky Way is our galaxy, an enormous system of billions of stars. Comets, planets and asteroids are much smaller objects.
quiz.placement: Explain: Classification Table, six rows on stars, planets, moons, comets, asteroids and galaxies with defining characteristics

quiz.prompt: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. Our solar system formed about 9 billion years after the Big Bang. About how many billion years ago did our solar system form?
choices: 13.8 billion years ago
9 billion years ago
4.8 billion years ago
22.8 billion years ago
quiz.rationale: The solar system formed 9 billion years after the Big Bang, so the time since then is 13.8 - 9 = 4.8 billion years. The age of the universe is not the same as the age of the solar system.
quiz.placement: Explain: Classification Table, 'Approximate Cosmic Age' column and checking that the age of the universe is not confused with the age of the solar system

quiz.prompt: After the classification activity, a learner wants to post a question on the Driving Question Board. Which question is the best scientific question that the class could investigate?
choices: Why are stars more beautiful than planets?
Why did God make the stars?
What evidence shows how far away each star is from Earth?
Is the night sky happy?
quiz.rationale: A testable question can be answered using evidence and measurement, such as distance data. The other questions are about purpose, opinion or feelings, which science cannot test.
quiz.placement: DQB: second sticky note with one new question raised by the classification activity

lessons.title: The Solar System: Structure and Scale

quiz.prompt: In the corridor model, each toilet paper square stands for 0.5 AU. One group's strip has a planet marked 8 squares from the Sun. How far is that planet from the Sun?
choices: 8 AU
16 AU
4 AU
2 AU
quiz.rationale: Each square is 0.5 AU, so 8 squares is 8 × 0.5 = 4 AU. Learners who answer 8 AU forget the scale, and those who answer 16 AU divide instead of multiplying.
quiz.placement: Observe: toilet-paper scaled model, calculating squares from the Solar System Distance Data Card

quiz.prompt: In a scale model of the Solar System, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars all lie within 1.52 AU of the Sun, while Neptune is 30.05 AU away. What does this show about the structure of the Solar System?
choices: The planets are spread out evenly, with about the same gap between each one
The outer planets are crowded together while the inner planets are far apart
The Solar System is mostly filled with planets and moons, with very little empty space
The four inner planets are bunched close to the Sun and most of the Solar System is empty space
quiz.rationale: All four inner planets fit within about 1.5 AU, while Neptune is 30 AU out. So the planets are clustered near the Sun and huge gaps separate them from the outer planets, leaving mostly empty space.
quiz.placement: Observe: walking the corridor and recording 'I noticed that ...' observations at the Neptune end

quiz.prompt: 1 AU is about 150 million km. Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun. About how far is Neptune from the Sun in kilometres?
choices: 450 million km
30 million km
4 500 million km
180 million km
quiz.rationale: Distance = 30 × 150 million km = 4 500 million km (4.5 billion km). One AU is the Earth–Sun distance, so 30 AU is 30 times as far.
quiz.placement: Observe: Solar System Distance Data Card, where 1 AU is about 150 million km and Neptune is 30.05 AU

quiz.prompt: The planets are tiny compared with the empty space around them, and nothing solid connects them to the Sun. What keeps a planet such as Jupiter orbiting the Sun instead of flying off into space?
choices: The Sun's gravitational pull toward the Sun, together with the planet's sideways motion, bends its path into an orbit
The asteroid belt acts like a barrier that stops the planets from drifting away
The planets are not moving sideways at all; they hang still because the Sun's gravity holds them in place
The Sun's heat pushes the planets so they stay at a fixed distance
quiz.rationale: The Sun's large mass pulls each planet inward. The planet also moves sideways at high speed, so the two together give a curved orbit rather than a straight-line escape or a crash into the Sun.
quiz.placement: Explain: class discussion 'what stops them from simply flying off in a straight line?' and force diagram of the Sun and Earth

quiz.prompt: A panga tied to a rope is swung in a circle, and the rope acts like the Sun's gravity on a planet. Suppose the Sun's gravity suddenly disappeared. What would Jupiter do?
choices: Stop moving and stay where it is
Keep moving in the same circle because it is used to orbiting
Move off in a straight line, like the panga when the rope breaks
Spiral inward and crash into the Sun
quiz.rationale: The inward pull is what bends the planet's path. With no pull, the planet would keep its sideways motion and travel in a straight line, as the panga does when the rope breaks.
quiz.placement: Explain: panga-on-a-rope analogy for orbital motion

quiz.prompt: Jupiter is about 5.2 AU from the Sun and Venus is about 0.72 AU away, yet both orbit the same Sun. Which statement explains this correctly?
choices: Jupiter stays in orbit only because it formed in the cold outer Solar System
The Sun's gravity still reaches Jupiter but is weaker there, so Jupiter moves more slowly than Venus and takes much longer to go round
The Sun's gravity does not reach Jupiter, so Jupiter is held in orbit by its own gravity
The Sun's gravity is stronger at Jupiter than at Venus, so Jupiter must move faster
quiz.rationale: Gravity weakens with distance but still acts across the whole Solar System. Venus feels a stronger pull and moves faster, while Jupiter feels a weaker pull and moves slower. The Sun's pull keeps bending both paths.
quiz.placement: Explain: written question (b) 'Why is Jupiter much farther from the Sun than Venus, yet both orbit the same Sun?'

quiz.prompt: A learner draws a Solar System model with arrows showing the gravitational force of the Sun on each planet. Which drawing is correct?
choices: Arrows pointing along the orbit, in the direction the planet is moving
No arrows are needed, because there is no force acting on planets in empty space
Arrows pointing from each planet toward the Sun, because gravity pulls the planets inward
Arrows pointing away from the Sun, because the Sun pushes the planets outward
quiz.rationale: The Sun's gravity pulls each planet toward the Sun. The idea that the Sun pushes planets away is a common misconception to correct.
quiz.placement: Model: adding gravity arrows to the Solar System Structure panel of the cumulative model

quiz.prompt: The Solar System has an asteroid belt at roughly 2.2 to 3.2 AU from the Sun. Mars is at 1.52 AU, Jupiter at 5.20 AU and Saturn at 9.58 AU. Where should the asteroid belt be drawn in a model?
choices: Beyond Neptune
Between Earth and Mars
Between Mars and Jupiter
Between Jupiter and Saturn
quiz.rationale: A distance of 2.2 to 3.2 AU is greater than Mars (1.52 AU) and less than Jupiter (5.20 AU), so the belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the asteroid belt to the Solar System Structure panel

quiz.prompt: In the PhET 'Gravity and Orbits' simulation, a planet is set moving around the Sun at a speed that is too high for a circular orbit. Which description of the path matches Kepler's First Law?
choices: An ellipse (oval) with the Sun at one focus, not at the centre
A perfect circle with the Sun exactly at the centre
A straight line that carries the planet away from the Sun
An ellipse with the Sun at the exact centre of the oval
quiz.rationale: Kepler's First Law says planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. The Sun is offset from the centre of the oval, so a circle or a centred ellipse is wrong.
quiz.placement: Task A: Orbit Shape (PhET 'Gravity and Orbits', Sun and Planet mode)

quiz.prompt: A planet moves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit. A learner shows the planet's velocity arrow at two points. Where is the planet moving fastest?
choices: At the same speed everywhere, because planets move at constant speed
Nearest to the Sun, where the velocity arrow is longest
Farthest from the Sun, because it has the most room to speed up
Halfway between the nearest and farthest points only
quiz.rationale: The planet moves fastest at perihelion, nearest the Sun, and slowest at aphelion, farthest from the Sun. This is the pattern behind Kepler's Second Law.
quiz.placement: Task B: Speed Variation (Kepler's Second Law) with Path and Velocity vectors

quiz.prompt: A data strip gives these orbital periods: Mercury 0.24 years (0.39 AU from the Sun), Earth 1.00 year (1.00 AU) and Jupiter 11.86 years (5.20 AU). Which pattern do the data show?
choices: The farther a planet is from the Sun, the shorter its orbital period
Orbital period does not depend on distance, only on the size of the planet
The farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its orbital period
All planets take about the same time to orbit the Sun
quiz.rationale: As distance increases from 0.39 to 1.00 to 5.20 AU, the period increases from 0.24 to 1.00 to 11.86 years. This is the qualitative pattern behind Kepler's Third Law.
quiz.placement: Task C: Period vs Distance (Kepler's Third Law, Qualitative)

quiz.prompt: Mars has an orbital period T = 1.88 years. What is T² for Mars, in years², when completing the Kepler's Third Law calculation table?
quiz.rationale: T² means T multiplied by itself: 1.88 × 1.88 = 3.53 years². Squaring is not the same as doubling (3.76), tripling (5.64) or taking a square root (1.37).
quiz.placement: Calculation table: T², r³ and T²/r³ for six planets

quiz.prompt: A learner calculates T²/r³ for Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, using T in years and r in AU. Every answer is close to 1.0. A graph of T² against r³ is also a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
choices: The planets all travel at the same speed in their orbits
All six planets are the same distance from the Sun
All six planets have the same orbital period
T² is proportional to r³ for all these planets, which verifies Kepler's Third Law
quiz.rationale: A constant ratio T²/r³ and a straight-line graph through the origin both show that T² is proportional to r³. This is Kepler's Third Law. The planets have different distances and periods.
quiz.placement: Calculation table and T² vs r³ graph with the CER paragraph

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'Earth has seasons because its elliptical orbit makes it much closer to the Sun in summer.' Which response is correct?
choices: Correct, because Earth is closest to the Sun in June
Correct, because Earth's orbit is a very long, thin ellipse
Incorrect, because Earth's orbit is almost circular and the seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis
Incorrect, because the Sun moves closer to Earth in summer
quiz.rationale: Earth's orbit is almost circular and Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by distance from the Sun.
quiz.placement: Formative assessment: common misconception about elliptical orbits and seasons

quiz.prompt: Using years for T and AU for r, T²/r³ = 1 for planets orbiting the Sun. A new object orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis r = 4 AU. What is its orbital period T?
choices: 4 years
64 years
16 years
8 years
quiz.rationale: T² = r³ = 4³ = 64, so T = √64 = 8 years. The answer 4 treats T as equal to r, 16 uses r², and 64 forgets to take the square root.
quiz.placement: After the whole lesson: applying Kepler's Third Law (T² ∝ r³) to a new orbit

quiz.prompt: The Moon travels around Earth and does not fly off into space in a straight line. Which statement explains this best?
choices: Earth's gravity pulls the Moon inward while the Moon keeps moving sideways, so it follows a curved path
Earth's magnetic field holds the Moon in place
Gravity pulls the Moon inward and an equal outward force pushes it away, so the two forces cancel
The Moon's own gravity pushes it away from Earth, and this keeps it at a steady distance
quiz.rationale: The only real force on the Moon is Earth's gravity pulling it inward. Because the Moon is also moving sideways, the pull bends its path into an orbit instead of letting it fall in or fly away. No outward force is needed.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on 'What stops the Moon from flying off into space in a straight line?'

quiz.prompt: A tide table for Mombasa Old Port shows these readings for Day 1: 00:12 h 3.1 m, 06:24 h 0.4 m, 12:48 h 3.0 m, 18:36 h 0.5 m. What pattern do the readings show?
choices: One high tide per day, so the sea is high once every 24 hours
Two high tides per day, roughly 12 hours apart
Four high tides per day, roughly 6 hours apart
The water level stays almost the same all day
quiz.rationale: The heights are high (3.1 m and 3.0 m) at 00:12 h and 12:48 h, which is about 12 hours apart. The low readings of 0.4 m and 0.5 m fall between them, so there are two high tides each day.
quiz.placement: Observe: Source A, Mombasa Old Port tidal height table (observation task 1)

quiz.prompt: Water on Earth bulges on the side facing the Moon and also on the opposite side at the same time. What explains the bulge on the far side?
choices: The Moon pulls Earth itself more strongly than it pulls the far-side water, so the far-side water is left behind and bulges outwards
Earth's spin throws water off only the side that faces away from the Moon
The Sun pushes the far-side water away from the Moon
The Moon pushes the far-side water away from itself
quiz.rationale: Gravity gets weaker with distance. The near-side water is pulled most, Earth's centre is pulled less, and the far-side water is pulled least. Earth moves towards the Moon more than the far-side water does, so the far-side water is left behind and forms a second bulge.
quiz.placement: Observe: Source B, Earth-Moon tidal bulge diagram (observation task 3 and the 'Why are there TWO tidal bulges?' question)

quiz.prompt: The Moon is moved to twice its present distance from Earth. Its mass does not change. By what factor does the gravitational force between Earth and the Moon change?
choices: It becomes 8 times weaker
It becomes 4 times weaker
It becomes 2 times weaker
It stays the same, because the masses have not changed
quiz.rationale: Gravitational force is proportional to 1/d². If d doubles, the force becomes 1/2² = 1/4 of its original value, so it is 4 times weaker.
quiz.placement: Explain: Explanation 2, inverse-square ratio activity, Problem A

quiz.prompt: The Sun has 27 million times the mass of the Moon and is about 390 times farther from Earth. Use F proportional to M divided by d² to compare their pulls on Earth. How does the Sun's pull compare with the Moon's pull?
choices: The Moon pulls harder, by about 390 times
The Sun pulls about 178 times harder
The Sun pulls about 69,000 times harder
The Sun pulls about 27 million times harder
quiz.rationale: Ratio = 27,000,000 ÷ 390² = 27,000,000 ÷ 152,100 ≈ 178. The Sun pulls on Earth about 178 times harder than the Moon does (roughly 180 times).
quiz.placement: Explain: Explanation 2, inverse-square ratio activity, Problem B (i)

quiz.prompt: Tidal effects depend on the difference in pull between the near and far sides of Earth. This difference is proportional to M divided by d³. The Sun has 27 million times the Moon's mass and is about 390 times farther away. Compared with the Moon's tidal effect, the Sun's tidal effect is about:
choices: 0.46 times as big, so about 46 percent of the Moon's
zero, because the Sun is too far away to cause tides
69,000 times bigger, because the Sun is so massive
180 times bigger, because the Sun pulls much harder
quiz.rationale: Ratio = 27,000,000 ÷ 390³ = 27,000,000 ÷ 59,319,000 ≈ 0.46. The Sun's tidal effect is about 46 percent of the Moon's, so the Moon raises the bigger tides, but the Sun's effect is not zero.
quiz.placement: Explain: Explanation 2, Problem B (ii), tidal effect and the M divided by d-cubed rule

quiz.prompt: The Moon pulls on the water of Lake Victoria just as it pulls on the Indian Ocean at Mombasa. Why does Lake Victoria show almost no tide?
choices: Lake Victoria is too far from the Sun to have tides
The Moon only pulls on salt water, not fresh water
The Moon's gravity cannot reach inland Africa
The lake is so small that the Moon's pull is almost the same across all of it, so the difference in pull is tiny
quiz.rationale: Tides come from the difference in the Moon's pull across a water body. Across a small lake that difference is tiny, so any tide is only a few millimetres to about a centimetre. Rain, wind and seiches cause larger changes.
quiz.placement: Explain: Explanation 3, Kenya connection (Mombasa and Lake Victoria contrast)

quiz.prompt: Proxima Centauri is about 40 trillion km from Earth. The fastest spacecraft ever built, the Parker Solar Probe, reaches about 700,000 km/h. Roughly how long would the journey take at that speed?
choices: About 65,000 years
About 6,500 years
About 650 years
About 65 years
quiz.rationale: Time = distance ÷ speed = 40 000 000 000 000 ÷ 700 000 ≈ 57 million hours. Dividing by 24 × 365 = 8 760 hours per year gives about 6,500 years, so travelling there is not practical and telescopes are needed.
quiz.placement: Predict: Proxima Centauri board prompt and the 6,500-year travel-time reveal

quiz.prompt: In a refracting telescope, parallel rays of light from a distant star pass through a convex objective lens. Where does the lens bring these rays together to form the image?
choices: At the star, where the light started
At the focal point, one focal length away from the lens
Nowhere; the rays stay parallel and spread out evenly
On the surface of the objective lens itself
quiz.rationale: A convex lens refracts parallel rays so they converge at the focal point, which is one focal length from the lens. The eyepiece then magnifies this image. Labelling the focal point on the lens itself is a common error.
quiz.placement: Observe, Component 1: ray diagram of a convex lens refracting parallel rays to a focal point

quiz.prompt: Why are the world's biggest modern optical telescopes reflecting telescopes (using mirrors) and not refracting telescopes (using lenses)?
choices: Mirrors detect radio waves, which lenses cannot
Lenses cannot bend light at all
Mirrors can be made very large and still keep their shape, while very large lenses are heavy and sag under their own weight
Light travels faster after it reflects from a mirror than after it passes through a lens
quiz.rationale: Large lenses are heavy and sag, which spoils the image. Mirrors can be much larger and still hold a precise shape. Lenses do bend light (refraction), and mirrors do not detect radio waves or speed light up.
quiz.placement: Observe, Component 1: comparing the refracting and reflecting telescope diagrams

quiz.prompt: The Hubble Deep Field image shows thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky about the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length. What does this image give us as evidence?
choices: The universe contains an enormous number of galaxies, even in a tiny part of the sky
An astronaut travelled to these galaxies and photographed them up close
All the objects in the image are stars inside our own Milky Way
The patch of sky was empty, so space is mostly nothing
quiz.rationale: Seeing thousands of galaxies in such a tiny patch shows that the universe is vast and full of galaxies. The evidence was gathered remotely by a telescope, not by travelling there.
quiz.placement: Observe, Component 2: video on the Hubble Space Telescope and the Hubble Deep Field

quiz.prompt: The MeerKAT telescope in South Africa, part of the Square Kilometre Array project, is a radio telescope. Which statement about radio telescopes is correct?
choices: They use large dish antennas to collect radio waves from galaxies and hydrogen clouds
They must be launched into space to work
They collect sound waves travelling through space
They use large lenses to bend visible light to a focal point
quiz.rationale: Radio telescopes use large dish antennas, not lenses or mirrors, to detect invisible radio waves emitted by galaxies and hydrogen clouds. Radio waves are not sound waves, and MeerKAT works from the ground in Africa.
quiz.placement: Explain: three-column comparison table (refracting, reflecting, radio telescope)

quiz.prompt: The James Webb Space Telescope detects infrared light from the first stars and galaxies, which formed over 13 billion years ago. What does this tell us about light and distance?
choices: The early universe is very close to Earth
The telescope travels back in time to collect the light
Light from very distant objects takes so long to reach us that we see those objects as they were long ago
Light from distant objects shows us how they look today
quiz.rationale: Light takes time to travel across space, so the light from very distant objects left them long ago. Telescopes therefore look back in time. Each telescope arrow in the model should point to the epoch of the objects it observes, not always to the Big Bang.
quiz.placement: Model Building: dotted timeline arrows from each telescope back to cosmic history

quiz.prompt: Complete the sentence in the best way: "Scientists gather evidence about distant stars and galaxies by..."
choices: waiting for the stars to move close enough to Earth to touch
sending astronauts to visit each star and bring back samples
using telescopes to collect light and other radiation, such as radio waves, that travel to us from distant objects
looking carefully with the naked eye, because it works as well as any instrument
quiz.rationale: Distant objects cannot be visited, so scientists collect the light and other radiation that reaches Earth, using refracting, reflecting and radio telescopes on Earth and in space.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: sticky note beginning "Scientists gather evidence by..."

lessons.title: History of Space Exploration: From Sputnik to the James Webb Telescope — and Kenya's Place in the Cosmos

quiz.prompt: A photograph shows a metallic sphere about the size of a basketball, covered in antenna rods. It was launched from Kazakhstan on 4 October 1957. What was this object?
choices: Voyager 1, the probe that took the first detailed images of the outer planets
Vostok 1, the spacecraft that carried the first human into space
Sputnik 1, the first human-made object to orbit Earth
The Hubble Space Telescope, which images distant galaxies
quiz.rationale: Sputnik 1 (1957) was the Soviet satellite that became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Vostok 1 (1961), Voyager (1977) and Hubble (1990) came later.
quiz.placement: Predict: Mystery Object Provocation (Sputnik 1 reveal)

quiz.prompt: Which list shows these four missions in the correct order, from earliest to latest?
choices: Sputnik 1, Vostok 1, Hubble Space Telescope, Apollo 11
Sputnik 1, Apollo 11, Vostok 1, Hubble Space Telescope
Sputnik 1, Vostok 1, Apollo 11, Hubble Space Telescope
Vostok 1, Sputnik 1, Apollo 11, Hubble Space Telescope
quiz.rationale: Sputnik 1 was launched in 1957, Vostok 1 in 1961, Apollo 11 in 1969 and Hubble in 1990.
quiz.placement: Observe: Mission Data Cards and observation table (timeline of missions)

quiz.prompt: The Kenya Space Agency (KSA) was founded in 2017 and is headquartered in Nairobi. In 2018 Kenya's first satellite, 1KUNS-PF, was launched. Where was it launched from?
choices: The International Space Station (ISS)
A launch pad in Nairobi
Kazakhstan, the same site as Sputnik 1
The surface of the Moon
quiz.rationale: 1KUNS-PF was launched from the International Space Station in 2018. It was not launched from Nairobi or from the Moon.
quiz.placement: Observe: 1-page briefing on the Kenya Space Agency (KSA)

quiz.prompt: SKA-Mid is being built in South Africa's Karoo, and its precursor MeerKAT already operates there. What kind of instrument is it, and what does it detect?
choices: A radio telescope array that detects radio waves from space
A satellite that measures the speed of rockets
An optical telescope in orbit that photographs visible light
A rover that collects rock samples from Mars
quiz.rationale: The Square Kilometre Array is a large array of radio telescopes. It detects radio waves from space and does not collect samples or orbit Earth.
quiz.placement: Observe: briefing on Africa's role in the Square Kilometre Array (SKA)

quiz.prompt: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) detects light that left a galaxy 13.5 billion years ago. What does this tell us?
choices: Distance and time are unrelated, so the image shows the galaxy as it is now
We see the galaxy as it looks today, because light from space arrives instantly
The galaxy is only 13.5 years old
We see the galaxy as it looked 13.5 billion years ago, because light takes time to travel across space
quiz.rationale: Light travels at a finite speed. Light from very distant objects shows them as they were long ago, so looking far away means looking back in time.
quiz.placement: Explain: anchor question 2 on JWST, light and distance

quiz.prompt: No human has touched a star or visited another galaxy. Which statement best explains how scientists have gathered evidence about the distant universe?
choices: Instruments such as telescopes and radio arrays detect light and radio waves that reach us from space
Scientists only use naked-eye observations from dark places like the Rift Valley
Astronauts have travelled to distant galaxies and brought back samples
Scientists guessed what the universe looks like, because it cannot be studied
quiz.rationale: Evidence about the distant universe is gathered indirectly. Instruments such as Hubble, JWST and radio arrays detect light and radio waves that travel to us.
quiz.placement: DQB: second half of the driving question on gathering evidence about a universe we cannot touch

quiz.prompt: A learner adds arrows to the 'Human Evidence Layer' of a universe model. Which mission and evidence pairing is correct?
choices: Voyager 1 & 2: lunar rock samples
Apollo 11: lunar rock samples brought back to Earth
Mars rovers: infrared images of the earliest galaxies
Hubble Space Telescope: first human in space
quiz.rationale: Apollo 11 (1969) was the first Moon landing and returned lunar rock samples. Voyager imaged the outer planets, Vostok 1 carried the first human, and JWST took the infrared images of the earliest galaxies.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the 'Human Evidence Layer' timeline bar with arrows linking missions to evidence

lessons.title: Space Phenomena and Effects on Earth: Solar Flares, Geomagnetic Storms, Eclipses, and Tidal Forces

quiz.prompt: On 11 May 2024, HF radio used for weather messages went silent and GPS positions jumped around. Which cause best explains this?
choices: The Sun's heat warmed Earth's surface and melted the radio signals
Charged particles and magnetic energy from a coronal mass ejection disturbed Earth's magnetic field and upper atmosphere
The Moon's gravity pulled radio waves away from the weather station
Earth's magnetosphere disappeared and let the Sun's light through
quiz.rationale: The blackouts came from a solar eruption (CME) that sent charged particles and magnetic disturbance towards Earth, not from heat or the Moon. The magnetosphere was compressed, not removed.
quiz.placement: Predict: scenario card about the silent HF radio channel and jumping GPS positions

quiz.prompt: A coronal mass ejection travels at 800 km per second. The Sun is 150 million km from Earth. About how long does the cloud take to reach Earth?
choices: About 52 hours
About 8 minutes
About 5 hours
About 187,500 hours
quiz.rationale: Time = distance ÷ speed = 150,000,000 ÷ 800 = 187,500 s. Dividing by 3600 gives about 52 hours, or roughly 2 days.
quiz.placement: Observe: case study handout Panel B (Journey Through Space)

quiz.prompt: A solar storm sends out two things at the same moment: electromagnetic radiation (radio waves and X-rays) and a cloud of charged particles (a CME). Which statement is correct?
choices: The radiation arrives in about 8 minutes, and the particle cloud arrives about 2 days later
Both arrive in about 8 minutes because they come from the same eruption
Both arrive at Earth together after about 2 days
The particle cloud arrives first because it is heavier
quiz.rationale: Electromagnetic radiation travels at the speed of light and takes about 8 minutes. The particle cloud travels at about 800 km/s and takes about 52 hours. They are two separate arrivals.
quiz.placement: Explain: cause-and-effect card sort (Cards 3, 4 and 5)

quiz.prompt: Earth's magnetosphere is hit by a strong CME during a geomagnetic storm. What does the magnetosphere do?
choices: It absorbs all the particles, so nothing reaches Earth's atmosphere
It deflects most of the charged particles, although some spiral towards the poles and it is compressed on the sunward side
It creates the charged particles that cause the storm
It has no effect, so the particles pass straight through to the ground
quiz.rationale: The magnetosphere protects Earth by deflecting most solar particles. In a storm it is compressed and some particles spiral towards the poles, causing auroras and disruption.
quiz.placement: Explain: card sort (Card 5 and Card 6, magnetosphere compressed and deflecting particles)

quiz.prompt: Why can a total solar eclipse be seen only from a narrow strip of Earth's surface?
choices: The Sun is switched off everywhere except along that strip
Earth's magnetosphere blocks the view everywhere else
The Moon's dark central shadow (umbra) that reaches Earth is small, so only places inside it see the Sun fully covered
Only that strip is facing the Moon's gravity
quiz.rationale: The Moon's umbra falls on only a small spot that sweeps across Earth as a narrow path. Places in the penumbra see only a partial eclipse.
quiz.placement: Explain: Eclipse Geometry board diagram (umbra and penumbra)

quiz.prompt: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 390 times farther away, so they look almost the same size in our sky. If the Moon were twice as far from Earth as it is now, what would happen?
choices: The Moon would look smaller than the Sun and could not fully cover it, so total solar eclipses would not happen
The Moon would look larger and total eclipses would last longer
Total eclipses would happen every month
Nothing would change, because the Moon's size in the sky depends only on the Sun
quiz.rationale: A more distant Moon looks smaller in the sky. It could no longer cover the Sun's whole disc, so only ring-shaped or partial eclipses would be seen.
quiz.placement: Explain: eclipse question 'If the Moon were twice as far away...' (30-second wait)

quiz.prompt: A strong geomagnetic storm happens in May 2024. Did it change the tides at Mombasa?
choices: Yes, because the Sun's charged particles pull the ocean upwards
No, because tides come from the Moon's (and Sun's) gravity, while the storm comes from the Sun's charged particles and magnetic field
Yes, because the storm heats the sea and makes the tides larger
No, because tides are caused by Earth's magnetosphere
quiz.rationale: Tides are caused by gravity, mainly the Moon's. A geomagnetic storm involves charged particles and magnetic fields, which are a different cause and do not change the tide cycle.
quiz.placement: Explain: Tides versus space weather question (did the May 2024 storm change the tides at Mombasa?)

quiz.prompt: When are the tides at Mombasa largest (spring tides)?
choices: When the Sun and Moon line up with Earth, at new moon and full moon
Only during a solar eclipse
During a geomagnetic storm
When the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other
quiz.rationale: When the Sun and Moon line up, the Sun's pull (about 46 percent of the Moon's) adds to the Moon's, so tides are largest at new and full moon.
quiz.placement: Explain: Tides versus space weather (Sun's pull and spring tides)

lessons.title: Careers in Space Physics: African and Kenyan Voices in the Cosmos

quiz.prompt: A Grade 10 student writes on a prediction card: "Space science is done in other countries. Kenyans do not work in space science." Which statement best corrects this belief?
choices: Kenyans can only work in space science if they first study abroad, because no Kenyan university teaches related courses.
Kenyan professionals work in space-related careers, for example at the Kenya Space Agency and the Kenya Meteorological Department.
Kenyans work only in telecommunications, never in satellite engineering or astrophysics.
Space science jobs in Kenya exist only in Nairobi and are not open to students from other counties.
quiz.rationale: Kenyan institutions such as the Kenya Space Agency, the Kenya Meteorological Department and universities such as the University of Nairobi and Strathmore University employ space professionals, and the career is open to any Kenyan student.
quiz.placement: Career Prediction Card: 'Do you think there are Kenyan professionals doing this job?'

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is Taifa-1, featured in the Satellite Engineering career cluster?
choices: A weather balloon launched by the Kenya Meteorological Department in 2023
A telescope at the University of Nairobi used to study the Big Bang
Kenya's first operational Earth-observation satellite, launched in 2023
A geostationary communications satellite owned by Safaricom
quiz.rationale: Taifa-1 is Kenya's first operational Earth-observation satellite, built by the Kenya Space Agency team and launched in 2023.
quiz.placement: Career cluster folders: Cluster 2 – Satellite Engineering (Kenya Space Agency, Taifa-1)

quiz.prompt: A group needs reliable information about the education pathway to become a satellite engineer in Kenya. Which source should they trust MOST?
choices: An unsigned social media post that says "anyone can do it without studying"
A forwarded message with no author or date
The Kenya Space Agency website and the course pages of a Kenyan university
A friend's memory of something a relative once said
quiz.rationale: Credible sources come from named, relevant institutions such as the Kenya Space Agency and universities. Anonymous posts, hearsay and forwarded messages cannot be checked.
quiz.placement: Career cluster folders: evaluating sources for credibility while completing the Career Profile Poster

quiz.prompt: Worldwide, about one in three researchers (about 33%) is a woman (UNESCO Institute for Statistics). Which conclusion is best supported by this lesson?
choices: Girls should avoid physics until more women work in space science.
Space science is only suitable for students from certain counties, which explains the lower share.
Women are less able than men at physics, which explains the lower share.
The idea that physics is not for girls is a myth. Women already work in space science and engineering, including in Africa, and ability, not gender, decides a person's path.
quiz.rationale: The lower share of women does not show lower ability. The lesson concludes that the belief that space science is not for girls is a myth, and that many women already work in space science, including in Africa.
quiz.placement: Structured whole-class PCI discussion on gender equity in space careers (UNESCO infographic)

quiz.prompt: Which sticky note is the strongest "blue" connection note linking a career to evidence from an earlier lesson?
choices: "I want to be a scientist one day."
"It connects to space."
"Space careers are interesting and exciting."
"Meteorologists use weather satellites in orbit, which links to our lesson on satellites, because the satellite images are what forecasters use."
quiz.rationale: A strong connection note names both a career and a specific concept from an earlier lesson. Here the meteorologist is linked to satellites in orbit sending images used for forecasts. The other notes are vague or give no link.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: three-colour sticky notes, blue 'connection' note

quiz.prompt: On a diagram of the universe, students label where each career works. Which career belongs at the LARGEST scale, the whole observable universe (Big Bang and cosmic microwave background)?
choices: Meteorologist
Cosmologist
Telecommunications engineer working with geostationary satellites
Satellite engineer building Earth-orbiting satellites
quiz.rationale: Cosmologists study the origin and evolution of the whole universe, including the Big Bang and the cosmic microwave background. The other careers work at Earth orbit or atmosphere scale.
quiz.placement: Human Network overlay: adding career labels at the correct scale on the cumulative 'How We Know' model

quiz.prompt: A student places "meteorologist at the Kenya Meteorological Department" at the galaxy scale on the model. Which correction is best?
choices: Move it to the scale of the Solar System, because forecasters measure the Sun's distance.
Leave it at the galaxy scale, because satellites collect data from other galaxies.
Move it to the scale of Earth's atmosphere, because meteorologists use data on weather and satellite images collected near Earth.
Move it to the scale of the whole universe, because weather forecasts depend on the Big Bang.
quiz.rationale: Meteorologists study Earth's atmosphere using satellite data (for example from EUMETSAT). The data is collected near Earth, not at galaxy distances.
quiz.placement: Human Network overlay: teacher check of career labels placed at scientifically appropriate scales

lessons.title: Consolidation and Evidence Review: Building a Coherent Narrative of the Universe

quiz.prompt: A Grade 10 learner writes a short story of the universe. Which list puts the events in the correct order, from earliest to latest?
choices: Big Bang, then expansion and cooling, then first stars, then the Solar System, then Earth
First stars, then the Big Bang, then Earth, then expansion and cooling, then the Solar System
Big Bang, then the Solar System, then first stars, then expansion and cooling, then Earth
Expansion and cooling, then Earth, then first stars, then the Big Bang, then the Solar System
quiz.rationale: The universe began in the Big Bang, then expanded and cooled. Stars formed next, and the Solar System and Earth formed later from material that earlier stars had made.
quiz.placement: Predict: 'Our Best Answer So Far' written narrative from the Lake Victoria prompt

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes what scientists mean by the Big Bang?
choices: The universe has always existed and has never changed
The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since
A giant star exploded about 13.8 thousand years ago inside space that was already empty
The Sun exploded and its pieces formed all the stars and planets
quiz.rationale: The Big Bang describes the start of the universe, including space and time, from a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. The universe has been expanding since then.
quiz.placement: Part: synthesis template, Group A anchor lessons 1 & 2 (Big Bang and evolution of the universe)

quiz.prompt: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
choices: Friction between the planets and space
The magnetic force of the Moon
The gravitational pull of Earth on all the planets
The gravitational pull of the Sun on each planet
quiz.rationale: The Sun's gravity pulls on each planet and keeps it moving in orbit. Kepler's Laws describe these orbits and gravity explains why they happen.
quiz.placement: Part: synthesis template, Group C anchor lessons 5 & 6 (Kepler's Laws, gravitational forces)

quiz.prompt: Scientists cannot travel back in time or visit distant galaxies. Which observation is indirect evidence that the universe began in a hot, dense state?
choices: Venus looks bright in the evening sky
Craters are visible on the surface of the Moon
Faint microwave radiation (the cosmic microwave background) reaches Earth from every direction in the sky
The Moon changes shape through the month
quiz.rationale: The cosmic microwave background is leftover radiation from the early hot universe. Telescopes detect it today, so it is indirect evidence for the Big Bang. The other observations do not show how the universe began.
quiz.placement: Part: synthesis template, Group D anchor lessons 7 & 8 (telescopes, history of space exploration) and gallery walk

quiz.prompt: How did the first stars form after the Big Bang?
choices: Gravity pulled clouds of hydrogen and helium gas together until they became hot and dense enough for nuclear fusion to start
Rocks inside the first planets caught fire and began to burn
Planets collided and joined together to make stars
Stars were made complete in the Big Bang and have not changed since
quiz.rationale: Gravity pulled clouds of gas together, which heated them until nuclear fusion started and the first stars began to shine. Planets formed later, so they cannot have made the first stars.
quiz.placement: Explain: 5-sentence 'Universe Narrative' paragraph (Big Bang to tonight's Nairobi sky)

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'The night sky above Nairobi looks the same every night, so the universe cannot have changed or had a beginning.' Which response is best?
choices: Scientists have travelled back to the Big Bang to see it for themselves

The changes happened over billions of years, which is far too slow to notice in one lifetime, and scientists use indirect evidence such as the cosmic microwave background and telescope observations to study them
The learner is correct because stars never change
The universe changed only in the last few years, so we cannot see it
quiz.rationale: The universe's history unfolds over billions of years, so the sky seems still to us. Scientists use indirect evidence gathered with telescopes to reconstruct that history.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: 'Final DQB Status Summary' and personal 'Knowledge Gain Statement'

quiz.prompt: A learner is labelling celestial bodies on a model of the Solar System. Which set of labels is correct?
choices: The Sun is a planet, Venus is a star and the Moon is a planet
The Sun is a star, Venus is a planet and the Moon is a natural satellite of Earth
The Sun is a planet, Venus is a natural satellite and the Moon is a star
The Sun is a star, Venus is a star and the Moon is a planet
quiz.rationale: The Sun is a star that makes its own light. Venus is a planet that orbits the Sun. The Moon is a natural satellite that orbits Earth. Venus looks bright but only reflects sunlight.
quiz.placement: Model: final revision of cumulative model (adding missing labels and correcting inaccurate annotations)

lessons.title: Model Building and Final Presentation: From the Big Bang to the Night Sky Above Nairobi

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 1, a learner wrote: "The night sky above Nairobi has always looked exactly like this, and it has always existed." Which statement best corrects this idea?
choices: Scientists estimate the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in the Big Bang, and stars and planets have formed and changed since then.
The stars were made at the Big Bang and have stayed exactly the same ever since.
The night sky is only a few thousand years old, because that is how long people have watched it.
Everything in the sky was made at the same moment about 4.6 billion years ago, and nothing has changed since.
quiz.rationale: The anchoring phenomenon is that the sky looks unchanging, but the evidence shows a universe about 13.8 billion years old that keeps changing. Stars are born, evolve and die, and planets formed much later.
quiz.placement: Predict Phase: annotating Lesson 1 'Our Starting Ideas' and Version 1 timeline

quiz.prompt: Scientists detect faint microwave radiation coming from every direction in space, called the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). What is this radiation evidence for?
choices: It is leftover energy from the very hot early universe, which supports the Big Bang.
It is heat from the Sun that has bounced off the planets.
It is light from the Milky Way's brightest stars, which supports stellar evolution.
It is radio signals sent by satellites orbiting the Earth.
quiz.rationale: The CMB is the cooled remnant of radiation from the hot, dense early universe. It is key evidence for the Big Bang.
quiz.placement: Observe Phase: Evidence Audit, checklist item 2 (CMB radiation as evidence for the Big Bang)

quiz.prompt: Hubble observed that the light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum (redshift). What does this observation show?
choices: The Earth is at the exact centre of the universe.
Galaxies are moving away from us, so the universe is expanding.
The distant galaxies are on fire and glowing red.
Distant galaxies are moving towards us and are getting closer.
quiz.rationale: Redshift means light waves are stretched because the source is moving away. Galaxies moving away from us is evidence that the universe is expanding.
quiz.placement: Observe Phase: Evidence Audit, checklist item 3 (Hubble's redshift observations and expanding universe)

quiz.prompt: Where did the carbon, oxygen and iron atoms in your body come from?
choices: They were all made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.
They were made inside the Earth's core and rose to the surface.
They were made inside stars and scattered into space when massive stars exploded as supernovae.
They were made by the Sun and sent to Earth as sunlight.
quiz.rationale: Heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron were forged in stellar cores and spread by supernovae. Only the hydrogen came mainly from the Big Bang.
quiz.placement: Observe Phase checklist item 4 and Model Phase Task 1, part (c): stellar evolution and heavier elements

quiz.prompt: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation says the force of gravity between two bodies depends on their masses and the distance between them. If the distance between two bodies is doubled, with the masses unchanged, what happens to the gravitational force?
choices: It becomes four times stronger.
It stays the same.
It becomes half as strong.
It becomes one quarter as strong.
quiz.rationale: Gravitational force is proportional to 1/r². Doubling r gives 1/2² = 1/4 of the original force.
quiz.placement: Observe Phase checklist item 7 (Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation and orbital mechanics) and Model Phase Task 1, part (e)

quiz.prompt: Scientists cannot travel to distant stars and galaxies. Which method do they mainly use to study them?
choices: Digging for rocks that fell from the stars to the ground.
Collecting samples of star material with rockets.
Collecting and analysing electromagnetic radiation such as visible light and radio waves using telescopes.
Measuring the sounds that stars make in space.
quiz.rationale: Distant objects are studied by detecting the electromagnetic radiation they send us, such as visible light, radio waves and the CMB, using telescopes.
quiz.placement: Explain Phase: Final Explanation presentations (types of telescopic and electromagnetic evidence)

quiz.prompt: On the Driving Question Board, a class marks a question YELLOW. What does a yellow dot mean?
choices: The question was wrong and should be removed.
It is a frontier question that no one can answer yet.
We have partial evidence, but the question needs more investigation.
We can fully answer it with evidence from our unit.
quiz.rationale: Green means answered with evidence, yellow means partly answered and needing more investigation, and red means still open.
quiz.placement: DQB Phase: traffic-light categorisation of Driving Question Board questions

quiz.prompt: According to the unit, how did our Solar System form?
choices: From a collapsing cloud (nebula) of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago.
From one giant star that split into the Sun and the planets.
The Sun formed first and then captured planets that came from other galaxies.
Directly from the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago.
quiz.rationale: The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing nebula. This was much later than the Big Bang, and the nebula contained material from earlier stars.
quiz.placement: Model Phase Task 1: Individual Written Reflection, part (d) (formation of the Solar System)

quiz.prompt: A person standing in the Rift Valley on a clear night looks up at the stars. Which statement best describes what they are seeing?
choices: A fixed pattern of lights that has never changed since the Big Bang.
Reflected light from the Moon only.
The stars exactly as they are at this very moment.
Ancient light that left objects long ago, giving a snapshot of a universe that is changing over billions of years.
quiz.rationale: Light takes time to travel, so we see stars as they were in the past. The night sky is a snapshot of a dynamic, evolving universe, not a static one.
quiz.placement: Model Phase Task 1, part (g) and Task 2: Whole-Class Synthesis of the Final Explanation

quiz.prompt: A group is building a causal chain from the Big Bang to the night sky above Nairobi. Which order is correct?
choices: Big Bang, then first stars and galaxies form, then massive stars end as supernovae and scatter heavier elements, then the Solar System forms.
First stars form, then the Big Bang, then supernovae, then the Solar System forms.
Big Bang, then the Solar System forms, then the first stars, then supernovae.
Solar System forms, then the Big Bang, then first stars, then supernovae.
quiz.rationale: Hydrogen clouds collapse into the first stars and galaxies after the Big Bang. Supernovae then scatter heavier elements, and later a nebula collapses to form the Solar System.
quiz.placement: Model Phase Task 2: Whole-Class Synthesis (sentence-by-sentence Final Explanation)
